unesco.title: Cheoyongmu
unesco.description: Cheoyongmu is a court dance today performed on stage but formerly used to dispel evil spirits and pray for tranquillity at royal banquets or during exorcism rites on New Year’s Eve to promote good fortune. Based on the Korean legend of Cheoyong, a son of the dragon king Yongwang, who took human form and saved his human wife from the smallpox spirit through singing and dancing, the dance is performed by five men clad in white, blue, black, red and yellow to represent the four cardinal directions and the centre. They wear the light wine-coloured mask of the man-god, with white teeth, tin earrings with a necklace of lead beads, and a black hat decorated with two peony blossoms and seven peaches to ward off evil and invite auspicious energy. The dancers move with stateliness and vigour through a variety of styles and tempos of music, punctuated by various lyrical song recitations. Part of a greater folk mythology surrounding Cheoyong, including the belief that his image carved on the gate of a house would repel smallpox and other ills, Cheoyongmu also embodies the philosophy of Confucianism, particularly the Theory of the Five Elements. The creation of the Cheoyong masks also provides a valuable opportunity for traditional craftsmanship.

profile.name: Cheoyongmu
profile.tagline: A majestic five-person court dance from Korea designed to dispel evil spirits.
profile.insight: Danced by five men in wine-colored masks with white teeth, Cheoyongmu applies the Theory of the Five Elements to ward off smallpox and invite good fortune.
profile.profile: Cheoyongmu is the oldest surviving Korean court dance, originating from the Unified Silla period. It features five dancers wearing distinct colored costumes representing the cardinal directions and the center. The dance serves both as a ritual to drive away evil spirits and a majestic display of traditional Korean court artistry, recognized globally by UNESCO.
profile.profile_long:
Cheoyongmu stands as the oldest surviving Korean court dance, tracing its origins back to the Unified Silla period. Rooted deeply in historical legend, the dance draws from the story of Cheoyong, a son of the dragon king Yongwang who assumed human form and courageously protected his wife from the smallpox spirit through song and movement. Historically, the dance carried a profound ritualistic weight, performed to drive off malevolent forces, ensure tranquility, and invite good fortune during New Year's Eve exorcism rites and royal banquets. While initially performed by a single dancer from the Silla period through the Goryeo dynasty, the tradition evolved into a magnificent five-person performance during the Joseon era, structured around the Confucian Theory of the Five Elements.

The performance is characterized by its visual splendor and rigorous symbolism. The five dancers are clad in distinct costumes representing the four cardinal directions and the center, utilizing the colors blue, white, black, red, and yellow. Their attire is complemented by light wine-colored masks of the man-god featuring white teeth, tin earrings paired with necklaces of lead beads, and black hats decorated distinctively with two peony blossoms and seven peaches—each element carefully chosen to ward off evil and welcome auspicious energy. The movement vocabulary is executed with stateliness and vigor, reacting to styles and tempos of music that are continually punctuated by lyrical song recitations.

Beyond the choreography itself, the tradition encompasses a vast web of folk mythology and traditional craftsmanship, including the creation of the iconic Cheoyong masks and the historical belief that carving Cheoyong's image on a house gate would repel smallpox and other ills. Though briefly interrupted by the annexation of 1910, the tradition was revived in the 1920s and has since transitioned from royal courts to contemporary stages. Today, Cheoyongmu is preserved not only as a pinnacle of South Korean Intangible Cultural Property, inscribed since 1971, but also as a masterpiece on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since 2009. Through its enduring custodians, the dance continues to embody ancient cosmological philosophies, offering a window into Korea's rich heritage of royal protection and ritualistic artistry.

sections.origins_and_history: Cheoyongmu originated during the Unified Silla period, making it the oldest surviving Korean court dance. It is based on the legend of Cheoyong, son of the dragon king Yongwang, who saved his wife from the smallpox spirit. From the Silla period to the late Goryeo dynasty, the dance was performed by a single dancer, after which it expanded to five dancers, incorporating the Confucian Theory of the Five Elements during the Joseon era.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is always performed by five dancers who move with stateliness and vigor. Specific footwork and arm movements are not described in sources. The performance is punctuated by various lyrical song recitations and adapts to the style and tempo of the accompanying music.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music accompanying Cheoyongmu features style and tempo variations punctuated by lyrical song recitations. Specific musical instruments are not named in the sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear costumes in yellow, red, blue, white, and black, representing the four cardinal directions and the center. They wear light wine-colored masks depicting a man-god with white teeth, tin earrings, lead bead necklaces, and black hats decorated with two peony blossoms and seven peaches.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Cheoyongmu was formerly performed during royal banquets, New Year's Eve exorcism rites to dispel evil spirits, and to pray for tranquility and good fortune. It embodies Korean folk mythology and the Confucian Theory of the Five Elements, including the belief that Cheoyong's image on a gate repels smallpox.
sections.notable_figures: Cheoyong, the mythological son of the Dragon King Yongwang.
sections.regional_variants: The dance transitioned from a single-dancer format in the Silla and Goryeo periods to a five-dancer format (Obang Cheoyongmu) during the Joseon era.
sections.lineage: Derived from Korean court dance traditions and shamanistic exorcism rituals of the Unified Silla period.
